glossary.def: A crystalline material only one or a few atoms thick, such as graphene. Its thinness gives it electronic, optical and mechanical properties unlike the bulk form.
A chemically modified RNA building block with an extra methyl group. Found in RNA caps and some transfer RNAs, where it helps stability and protein production.
Adeno-associated virus: a small, mild virus that is stripped of its own genes and used as a vehicle to deliver therapeutic genes into cells.
The rule that a material that absorbs light strongly also emits it strongly. In solar cells it means good absorbers tend to lose energy quickly by emitting light.
A small, simple marine worm without a gut cavity. Some species host algae in their bodies and are used to study regeneration and symbiosis.
A protein that assembles into thin filaments forming much of a cell's internal scaffold; growing networks of it push membranes and drive cell movement.
The part of the daily cycle when an animal is awake and active, which in mice is the night.
The mixing of genetic ancestry when previously separate populations interbreed.
Tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in air, which scatter light, seed cloud droplets and carry nutrients and pollutants.
Slow, quiet sliding on a fault in the months and years after an earthquake, continuing to release stored stress.
A genus of gut bacteria that feeds on the gut's mucus layer. Akkermansia muciniphila is linked to metabolism and responses to immunotherapy.
A rapid build-up of algae in water. When one collapses, much of the carbon the algae captured is either released again or sinks into deep water.
A nitrogen-containing plant compound, often biologically active. Caffeine, morphine and nicotine are familiar examples.
The ability of an organism to tell its own cells or tissues from those of genetically different members of the same species.
Attaching a three-carbon unit containing a double bond to a molecule, a common way to set up later ring-forming steps.
A deep-learning system that predicts the three-dimensional shape of proteins, and in later versions other molecules, from their sequence.
A type of magnet whose atomic magnetic moments cancel out overall, like an antiferromagnet, yet whose electrons still behave as if spin-split, as in a ferromagnet.
Joining a gene's coding pieces in different combinations, so one gene can yield several different messenger RNAs.
A solid built from silicon, aluminium and oxygen; substituting aluminium for silicon creates acidic sites useful in catalysis.
Repeated automatic blood pressure readings taken over a full day and night while a person goes about normal life, used as the reference standard for diagnosis.
An almond-shaped group of nerve cells deep in each side of the brain that helps process emotions, especially fear and threat.
A type of protein clump in which many copies of a protein stack into long, stable fibres. Often linked to disease, but some amyloids do normal jobs in cells.
Genetic material recovered from old remains such as bones and teeth, used to study past populations and their movements.
A weak steroid hormone made by the adrenal glands and ovaries that the body converts into testosterone or oestrogen.
A state in which an immune cell meets its target but cannot respond, leaving it present yet functionally silenced.
The tough, layered outer ring of a spinal disc, built from angled collagen sheets that contain the soft core under load.
A magnet whose neighbouring atomic moments point in opposite directions, so the material is ordered but shows little net magnetism.
Reduction of the body's detection of or response to painful stimuli, as measured in animal studies.
A short synthetic nucleic acid designed to stick to a chosen RNA and block or redirect how it is used.
A small flowering plant in the mustard family (thale cress), used as the standard model organism in plant biology because of its small genome and short life cycle.
A single-celled microbe without a nucleus that forms a separate domain of life from bacteria. Some groups are the closest known relatives of complex cells.
A transcription factor that drives neuroendocrine identity in nerve-like cells and defines a major subtype of small cell lung cancer.
A lab-grown 3D tissue model that combines different cell types or mini-organs, such as tumour cells with their supporting cells.
A late stage of a moderate-mass star when it has swollen enormously, burns shells around an inert core and loses mass in strong winds.
A lack of shared timing, so different places or individuals go through the same seasonal stage at different times.
A sequencing method that finds which parts of the genome are open and accessible, which marks DNA regions likely to control gene activity.
The conveyor of Atlantic water that carries warmth north at the surface and returns cold water south at depth, shaping regional climate.
A method that strips atoms one by one from a needle-shaped sample and identifies them, giving a three-dimensional map of composition.
A reaction where a catalyst moves a halogen atom so that a radical joins across a carbon-carbon double bond, making a single new product.
A controlled way to make plastics in which a metal catalyst switches growing polymer chains on and off by moving a halogen atom.
Scanning a sharp tip across a surface and measuring the tiny forces on it, giving images and stiffness measurements of soft samples at fine scale.
The loss of signal strength as a wave travels through a material, because energy is absorbed or scattered along the way.
A billionth of a billionth of a second. Laser pulses this short can capture the motion of electrons.
Comparing a signal with a delayed copy of itself. In optics this is used to measure how short a pulse is.
A way for software to compute exact derivatives of its own calculations, which is what lets models with millions of parameters be fitted.
A family of protein machines, also called SWI/SNF, that move or loosen packaged DNA to control gene access. Its genes are often mutated in cancer.
A property of a material's electron energy bands, described by whole-number invariants, that stays the same under smooth changes and leads to protected edge or surface states.
The energy gap an electron must jump to conduct electricity in a solid. Metals have no gap, semiconductors a small one, insulators a large one.
Gene editing that chemically converts one DNA letter into another at a chosen spot, without cutting both strands of the double helix.
The rule-bound pairing of nucleotides that holds the two strands of DNA together and folds RNA into its working shapes.
Years counted backwards from year 1 of the standard calendar; the same numbering as BC, used as a neutral label in archaeology and history.
Dating convention counting years back from 1950, the reference year used for radiocarbon results.
A late Stone Age to Bronze Age culture across much of Europe, named for its distinctive pottery and linked to large-scale population movement.
An experiment measuring correlations between separated systems to show they cannot be explained by any pre-agreed classical instructions.
A fixed set of tasks with known answers, used to compare systems. Scores need not carry over to real-world use.
A fibre built from chained glucose units, found in oats, barley, mushrooms and yeast. The cereal form dissolves, thickens gut contents and feeds gut bacteria.
A member of the BCL-2 protein family that senses stress and switches on the proteins that puncture mitochondria, starting programmed cell death.
Tetrahydrobiopterin: a helper molecule needed by several enzymes that make neurotransmitters and nitric oxide. It also acts as an antioxidant in cell membranes.
A molecule made from cholesterol in the liver that helps digest fats. Gut bacteria modify bile acids into forms with different signalling effects.
The total mass of living material in a group or place, used as a measure of how much of a population there is.
A compound of bismuth and sulfur that behaves as a semiconductor. It absorbs visible light well and is studied for solar cells and light detectors.
A tight lining of blood vessels in the brain that controls which substances pass from blood into brain tissue.
The internal timekeeper that runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle and times sleep, hormone release and other daily rhythms; it is reset mainly by light.
A state in which a cloud of atoms is cooled so far that they all occupy the same lowest quantum state and act as one wave.
A rubbery material made of backbone chains carrying dense side branches, which keeps it very soft while remaining a solid.
A wave state that stays trapped and does not leak away even though its energy lies within a range of freely moving states. Known in optics and now sought in electronics.
A system that reads brain signals and turns them into control of a device or into text or speech, used to restore lost function.
The basic range of electron momentum values in a crystal. Plotting electron energies across it shows a material's electronic band structure.
An increase in the number of repeated CAG DNA units in a gene. In Huntington's disease, longer repeats cause disease, and repeats can keep lengthening in some cells over life.
Measuring the heat taken up or given out by a process, used to follow reaction rates, energy changes and safety limits.
A connective-tissue cell in a tumour that has been changed by cancer cells and helps shape tumour growth, immune responses and drug response.
The protein shell that packages a virus's genetic material and protects it until it reaches the next host cell.
A T cell engineered to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, which lets it recognise and kill cells with a chosen surface target, used against blood cancers.
A molecule containing a carbon atom with only two bonds and two unshared electrons, often reactive and sometimes magnetic.
A positively charged, electron-poor carbon species formed as a short-lived intermediate; it reacts fast and can trigger ring-forming chains of steps.
The money needed to avoid one tonne of carbon dioxide emissions. A negative value means the cleaner option is cheaper than the one it replaces.
One of 23 standard stages used to describe human embryo development over the first eight weeks, based on visible features rather than exact age.
A small molecule, rich in red meat, that carries fatty acids into mitochondria so they can be burned for energy.
A widespread black crow of Europe and Asia, Corvus corone. Crows are highly intelligent birds used in studies of cognition.
A protein-cutting enzyme that executes programmed cell death. Some deaths proceed even when caspases are blocked.
A surface protein found on almost all B cells, used as the target for engineered cell therapies that remove them.
A rare type of dendritic cell that is especially good at showing fragments of dying tumour or infected cells to killer T cells and starting their response.
The layered boundary of a bacterium, including membrane and wall, which sets what gets in and how the cell resists attack.
The ability of a cell to switch its identity or behaviour without changing its DNA, letting tumours and tissues shift between states.
A permanent arrest of cell division after damage or stress. The cells persist and secrete signals that drive ageing and inflammation.
A small, stable statistical area used for reporting census data, roughly neighbourhood-sized, below the county level.
A network of nerve cells that produces rhythmic output, such as walking, breathing or swimming movements, without needing rhythmic input from the senses or brain.
A group of marine molluscs including squid, octopus and cuttlefish, known for large brains and complex behaviour.
The prehistoric period when copper was first worked but stone tools were still in general use, between the Stone and Bronze Ages.
A helper protein that assists other proteins in folding into the right shape, prevents them from clumping, and helps refold or clear damaged ones.
A frozen, periodic ripple in electron density across a material, competing with superconductivity for the same electrons.
Cancer treatment with drugs that block brake molecules on T cells, such as PD-1 or CTLA-4, so the immune system attacks tumours more strongly.
Binding a metal ion by gripping it at several points of one molecule at once, which holds it tightly and can block its reactivity.
Putting engineered receptors into chosen cells so a normally inert drug can switch just those cells on or off in a living animal.
An insulating material whose interior blocks current while protected channels carry it along the edges, labelled by a whole-number topological index.
A metallic state whose electron bands carry a nonzero topological whole-number invariant, so it shows a strong Hall effect and edge currents while its interior still conducts.
A conducting channel along the edge of a topological material in which electrons travel in only one direction, so they resist backscattering.
A magnetic arrangement in which the atomic moments rotate steadily along one direction with a fixed handedness, like a corkscrew.
Handedness: the property of an object or motion that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, like left and right hands. Applies to molecules, crystals and waves.
A gut hormone released after eating that slows the stomach and signals fullness. It also marks certain neuron types in the brain.
DNA together with the proteins that package it in the nucleus; how tightly it is wound controls access for reading and copying genes.
How open or loosely packed a stretch of DNA is. Open regions can be reached by proteins that switch genes on or off.
A method that uses antibodies to pull down a chosen protein with the DNA it is bound to, showing where that protein sits on the genome.
A folded stretch of DNA that brings two distant sites, such as a gene's start and a control region, into contact.
A DNA variant linked to how open a nearby stretch of chromatin is. Helps explain how variants outside genes affect gene control.
A single-celled organism covered in short beating hairs used for swimming and feeding, common in guts, soil and water.
The difference in how a material absorbs left- and right-circularly polarised light. It reveals handedness in molecules or, in magnetic materials, the direction of magnetisation.
A cancer cell that has broken away from a tumour and travels in the blood. Such cells can seed metastases.
Small pieces of DNA released by tumours into the blood. Measured by blood test to track cancer, treatment response or remaining disease.
Electrical stimulation that is adjusted automatically from signals measured in the body, so delivery tracks the current state instead of running on a fixed setting.
A spore-forming bacterium that makes many toxins and can cause food poisoning, gas gangrene and gut infections.
A single-celled marine alga that builds plates of chalk around itself. Their blooms and sinking plates move large amounts of carbon.
A group of three nucleotides that specifies one amino acid, the unit in which the protein-making machinery reads messenger RNA.
An emotion-control strategy of rethinking the meaning of a situation to change how one feels about it.
How long a wave or quantum state keeps a steady phase relationship with itself before it is scrambled.
A ring-shaped protein complex that holds copied chromosomes together and extrudes DNA loops that organize the genome in 3D.
Carbon-rich residue that builds up on a catalyst during high-temperature processing of oil, blocking pores and reducing activity.
An atom cooled with lasers and magnetic fields to near absolute zero, so its quantum behaviour can be controlled and used to model other systems.
Describes microbes that live on or in a host normally without causing harm, such as the usual bacteria of the skin and gut.
A stage in a close pair of stars where both end up inside one shared outer gas layer, dragging them together and often ejecting that gas.
A DNA difference carried by a sizeable share of the population, usually more than about one percent. Each one typically has only a small effect on disease risk.
A pair of small dense remnants such as white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes orbiting closely around each other.
Triggering of the complement system, a cascade of blood proteins that tags and destroys microbes and drives inflammation. Uncontrolled activation can damage the body's own tissues.
The basic unit of electrical conductance for one perfect channel in a nanoscale conductor, set by fundamental constants.
A complete wiring map of all nerve cells and their connections in a nervous system or part of it.
A feature of quantum measurements whereby results cannot all be assigned in advance independently of which other measurements are made alongside them.
The splitting of a continent into separate pieces by stretching of its crust, which can lead to formation of a new ocean basin.
A small wearable sensor that reads tissue glucose every few minutes, replacing intermittent finger-prick tests.
Two electrons bound into a pair. When pairs move in step, the material carries current with no resistance.
The set of atoms directly bonded around a metal ion, whose number and arrangement set its reactivity and catalytic behaviour.
A stretch of DNA that is deleted or duplicated, so a cell has fewer or more copies of it than usual.
An attachment that blocks a star's glare inside a telescope so much fainter nearby objects, such as planets, become visible.
A large, structured collection of texts or recordings gathered for systematic analysis, as of a language or animal songs.
The material placed between an ultrasound probe and the skin so sound passes through instead of reflecting off trapped air.
Breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more valuable ones, usually with heat and an acidic catalyst.
A gene-editing system adapted from bacterial immunity in which a guide RNA leads an enzyme such as Cas9 to a chosen DNA site to cut or change it.
Using a guided, cutting-disabled targeting protein fused to switch-on factors to raise a chosen gene's output without changing the sequence.
Use of a disabled CRISPR protein to sit on a gene and block its reading, dialling expression down instead of cutting the DNA.
An experiment that uses CRISPR gene editing to switch off many genes, one per cell, to find which genes matter for a chosen effect.
The temperature below which a material becomes superconducting, or more generally at which it switches into an ordered phase.
A molecule that ties neighbouring filaments or polymer chains together, making a network hold its shape and resist deformation.
Imaging rapidly frozen molecules with an electron beam and averaging many particle views to build a detailed three-dimensional structure.
Imaging frozen biological samples from many tilt angles with an electron microscope and combining the views into a three-dimensional picture.
A DNA-binding protein that marks boundaries in the genome and helps fold DNA into loops, shaping which genes and control regions meet.
Deliberately killing part of a wild population, sometimes proposed to protect another species or to control numbers.
A copper-oxide compound. Several cuprates superconduct at unusually high temperatures, and why is still argued over.
Photosynthetic bacteria, once called blue-green algae, that put oxygen into Earth's early atmosphere and still bloom in water today.
A reaction in which a molecule joins two of its own parts to close a ring.
An inherited mitochondrial disorder in which the last enzyme complex of the electron transport chain (complex IV) works poorly, often affecting brain, muscle, heart and liver.
A large family of iron-containing enzymes that add oxygen to molecules, important in drug breakdown and in building natural products.
The central part of the periodic table holding the transition metals, whose partly filled inner electron shells make them versatile catalysts.
A molecule released from damaged or stressed cells, or from microbes, that warns the immune system and triggers inflammation.
A genus of tiny freshwater fish related to zebrafish that stay transparent and have a small brain as adults, making them useful for imaging the whole animal.
Searching large datasets with automated methods to find patterns, relationships or candidates that would be hard to spot by hand.
An antibody-drug conjugate that uses an antibody against the protein TROP2 to deliver a cell-killing drug directly to cancer cells.
An enzyme that removes a carboxyl group from a molecule, releasing carbon dioxide and converting one small compound into another.
The habit of shedding leaves for part of the year, usually in a dry or cold season, instead of keeping them all year round.
A drug that removes a disease-related protein by steering the cell's own protein-destruction machinery onto it, instead of simply blocking the protein's activity.
The spreading of electrons over many atoms or a whole material rather than being tied to one atom or bond. It underlies metallic conduction and long-range electronic effects.
Breaking a polymer back down into its small building blocks, which can enable true recycling.
The settling of gases and particles from the air onto land or water, delivering nutrients or pollutants to ecosystems.
A heavier form of hydrogen with an extra neutron. It behaves almost like ordinary hydrogen, so it is used as a traceable stand-in.
A biological cycle that follows the 24-hour day-night cycle, for example changes in activity or behaviour between day and night.
An intermediate omega-6 fatty acid sitting between linoleic acid and arachidonic acid in the body's fat-processing chain.
A single-celled, mostly marine alga, often with two whip-like tails. Some live inside animals such as corals and supply them with food made by photosynthesis.
The direct magnetic interaction between two magnetic moments through space, like the pull between two small bar magnets. It is weak but can split energy levels.
A retinal output neuron that responds strongly to movement one way across the visual field and weakly to the opposite way.
The movement of individuals away from where they were born to new places to live and breed. It links populations and spreads genes.
A collection of many genetically different lines or varieties of a species, studied together to link natural genetic differences to traits.
A short DNA construct built to change shape when a binding event happens, turning that event into a readable signal.
A huge mixture of small molecules, each tagged with its own DNA barcode, so winners from a screen can be identified by sequencing.
A narrow boundary separating two regions of a material or field that have settled into different but equally favourable states.
Adding or removing electrons in a material, by chemical substitution or an electric gate, to tune its properties. Removing electrons creates holes.
A side effect severe enough to prevent raising a drug's dose any further, used in early trials to find a safe dose.
A setting in which two neighbouring subduction zones operate side by side, with two plates sinking into the mantle and interacting.
The fruit fly genus, especially Drosophila melanogaster, a small insect widely used in genetics and biology because it breeds fast and is easy to modify genetically.
Slow rise and fall of the land surface caused by flow in the mantle beneath it, rather than by plate collisions.
A technique that applies a sequence of control pulses to a qubit to cancel out noise from its surroundings and extend its coherence.
An unhealthy imbalance in the community of microbes living in the body, such as the gut, compared with a normal state.
A large protein that links the inner skeleton of muscle cells to their surrounding membrane, protecting fibres during contraction. Its loss causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
An enzyme that attaches ubiquitin tags to specific target proteins, often marking them for destruction. Hundreds of different types decide which proteins are tagged.
Adversity during infancy or childhood, such as isolation or neglect, which can leave lasting changes in brain circuits and later sensitivity.
A computer representation of the species and physical conditions of a region, used to predict how changes ripple through the whole system.
The part of a membrane protein that sticks out of the cell and usually binds signals or neighbouring cells.
A swirl of circulating fluid within a larger flow; disordered flows hold swirls of many sizes that mix material.
Internal force per unit area in a material that is being stretched or squeezed but will spring back when released.
Heating when a material is squeezed or stretched and cooling when released, a basis for refrigeration without gases.
Speeding up a chemical reaction at an electrode with a small applied voltage, so electricity does the work of a reagent.
A treatment that works by delivering electrical stimulation to nerves or tissue rather than by giving a drug.
Chemistry driven by or producing electric current at electrodes, the basis of batteries, electrolysis and many synthetic methods.
The jumping of electrons from one atomic site to a neighbouring one in a solid; the pattern of hops shapes the material's energy bands.
A computational imaging method that recovers structure from overlapping electron scattering patterns, reaching very fine resolution in thin samples.
A series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane that pass electrons along and pump protons, creating the energy store used to make ATP.
When an excited electron in a semiconductor falls back and fills an empty state, called a hole, losing its energy as light or heat. Slow loss helps solar cells.
A small unit of energy: the energy one electron gains when moved across a voltage of one volt. Widely used for bond, band and particle energies.
The ability of a reaction to make one mirror-image form of a product in preference to the other.
Found naturally only in one place, such as a single island or region, and nowhere else.
The process by which a cell takes in material from outside by folding its membrane inward to form a small bubble inside the cell.
Overload of the cell compartment that folds proteins. Prolonged overload triggers alarm pathways that can end in cell death.
A stretch of DNA, often far from the gene it controls, that boosts how much that gene is switched on in a particular cell type.
A gene an organism cannot live without under given conditions, so losing it stops growth. Such genes are favoured as drug targets.
Surviving a hot or dry season in a dormant state with slowed metabolism, the warm-weather counterpart of hibernation.
An organism whose cells have a nucleus and other internal membrane-bound compartments, including animals, plants, fungi and many single-celled forms.
The time after treatment during which a patient has no defined bad event, such as cancer growth, return or death.
A search method that keeps many candidate solutions, scores them, and makes new ones by copying and mutating the best, repeating over generations.
A hybrid of light and a bound electron-hole pair in a material, behaving as a very light particle that interacts strongly with its neighbours.
A T cell that has lost much of its killing and multiplying ability after long exposure to antigen, as in chronic infection or cancer.
A DNA variant linked to how much a gene is expressed. Used to connect disease-linked variants to the genes they likely affect.
A pair of facing mirrors or reflecting edges that trap light bouncing between them, selecting sharp wavelengths set by the spacing.
A common way metal atoms pack, with atoms at the corners and face centres of a cube. The arrangement governs strength and ductility.
A state that looks stable but is not the lowest-energy one, so it can eventually tunnel to the true minimum, releasing energy.
Enzymatic insertion of double bonds into a fatty acid chain, which changes how fluid and how oxidation-prone a membrane is.
The observation that females need a heavier genetic burden than males to develop some conditions, notably autism, suggesting a buffering mechanism.
A cloud of particles such as atoms or electrons that obey the rule forbidding two of them from sharing the same quantum state.
A form of regulated cell death driven by iron and the damaging oxidation of fats in cell membranes. It differs from apoptosis.
A fine thread-like bundle of protein molecules. Collagen fibrils are the load-bearing threads of tendon, bone and disc.
How closely something produced matches what was intended, such as a prepared quantum state compared with the target state, or a copied DNA sequence compared with its template.
A measure of solar cell quality: the most power it can deliver divided by the product of its highest voltage and highest current. Higher means fewer losses.
Statistical analysis that narrows a disease-linked DNA region down to the variants most likely to actually cause the effect.
Describes the first clinical study in which a new drug or treatment is given to people after laboratory and animal testing.
An electron energy band whose energy hardly changes with momentum, so electrons move very slowly and interactions dominate, often producing unusual states.
Adding fluorine atoms to a molecule. It is widely used in drug and agrochemical synthesis because fluorine changes stability and how a compound behaves in the body.
A carbon chain carrying fluorine atoms. Adding such groups to a drug or material changes stability, greasiness and binding.
A grid of light-sensing pixels placed at the focus of a lens, forming the image sensor of a camera, especially an infrared one.
The network of who eats whom in a community, through which a change in one group spreads indirectly to many others.
A small positively charged organic ion widely used in the crystal lattice of halide solar-cell absorbers, where it affects stability and light absorption.
A gene switched on quickly when cells, including nerve cells, are stimulated. Its protein is widely used as a marker of recently active neurons.
A large model pretrained on broad data, then adapted to many specific tasks instead of being trained separately for each one.
Scanning an electron beam across a thin sample and recording a full scattering pattern at every point, mapping structure and strain at atomic scale.
A condition where the number of electrons per repeating cell is a fraction rather than a whole number, which favours exotic states.
Light or microwave output made of many evenly spaced sharp frequencies, used as a precise ruler for measuring frequencies and time.
A specific group of atoms within a molecule, such as a hydroxyl or amine group, that gives the molecule its characteristic chemical reactions.
A brain scanning method that tracks changes in blood oxygen to show which brain areas are more active during a task.
A protein that, once cut, punches pores in the cell membrane and drives the inflammatory cell death called pyroptosis.
A group of genes sitting next to one another on a chromosome whose products work in the same pathway, often switched on together.
Making targeted changes to the DNA of living cells, such as cutting, deleting or rewriting a specific sequence, often with CRISPR-based tools.
Movement of genetic variants between populations through migration and interbreeding.
The amount of genetic variation within a species or population. Higher diversity helps populations adapt to change and avoid inbreeding problems.
The gradual loss of genetic variation in a population or species, often from shrinking or isolated populations, which can go unnoticed while numbers still look healthy.
A tissue containing cells of two or more genotypes, used experimentally so edited and normal cells can be compared side by side.
Building and installing large stretches of designed or human-derived DNA into a cell's chromosomes, rather than editing single letters.
A study that scans DNA markers across the whole genome in many people to find variants that are more common in those with a trait or disease.
Routinely sequencing pathogens from patient samples and linking the results to who, when and where, to follow spread and detect new variants.
The use of earth science methods, such as study of sediments and landforms, to understand past human activity and environments.
Precise measurement of the Earth's shape and of how its surface moves, now done with satellites and seafloor instruments.
A computer simulation of how rock in the Earth's interior deforms and flows over geological time, used to test what forces move plates and shape the surface.
The Earth's own magnetic field, generated in its liquid core, which many animals use as a cue for orientation and long-distance travel.
Comparing shapes by measuring landmark points on specimens and analysing them statistically, so subtle differences in form can be quantified.
The salt of gluconic acid, a harmless oxidised form of glucose that the kidneys clear in urine.
A small dry bract enclosing the flower or grain of a grass; its size and shape are important traits in cereals.
A protein carrying attached sugar chains. On virus surfaces, glycoproteins grip host receptors and drive entry into the cell.
A cell in the developing gonad that surrounds and nurtures germ cells; it becomes a Sertoli cell in testes or a granulosa cell in ovaries and directs sex development.
Glutathione peroxidase 4: an enzyme that repairs oxidised fats in cell membranes. It is the main protector against ferroptosis.
The interface where two differently oriented crystal grains in a solid meet; it is often where defects gather and failure starts.
A very small neuron. In the cerebellum these are the most numerous neurons in the brain and relay incoming signals to Purkinje cells.
An enzyme released by killer T cells and natural killer cells that enters target cells, usually through perforin pores, and triggers their death.
A single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern. It is extremely thin, strong and conducts electricity very well.
A regularly ridged or grooved structure that reflects, splits or steers light by interference, used to couple beams in and out of devices.
A widespread gap in the rock record where ancient basement rock lies directly beneath much younger sediment, marking enormous lost erosion.
A state in which three or more systems are all linked together so that measuring them shows correlations impossible for independent parts.
A small smoky-smelling aromatic compound produced when microbes break down plant material; it is a volatile cue detected by some insects.
A small nitrogen-rich compound that almost always carries a positive charge, which makes it hard to modify chemically.
The breaking up of a continuous natural habitat into smaller, isolated patches, often by farming, roads or building, which cuts animal movement and gene flow.
The bone-marrow cell that renews itself and gives rise to every type of blood cell.
The voltage across a conductor, sideways to the current, divided by the current, when a magnetic field is applied. Its quantized values reveal topological states.
A set of gene variants on one chromosome region that are inherited together as a block from one parent.
The part of life spent in good health, free of serious disease or disability, as opposed to total lifespan.
A group of Asgard archaea, microbes thought to be among the closest living relatives of the ancestor of all complex cells.
A molecule made of linked rings that twist into a spiral, giving it a left- or right-handed shape.
A long straight-chain hydrocarbon found in the waxy coating of insects, where such compounds act as contact chemical signals.
One of a family of proteins that coat newly made RNA and help decide its splicing, location and stability.
The boundary between two different materials in a device, where electronic levels and defects determine how charge crosses.
An electrically insulating layered crystal with a honeycomb lattice, used as an atomically flat support or spacer for thin conducting sheets.
A sequencing method that captures which parts of the genome touch each other in 3D space, used to map genome folding.
A diet in which a large share of calories comes from fat, used in animal studies to cause obesity or study how nutrition affects metabolism and inflammation.
The intricate pattern of allowed electron energies that appears when a lattice is placed in a strong magnetic field.
A film in a solar cell that lets positive charges pass out to the electrode while blocking negative ones, keeping the two kinds of carrier apart.
An animal's ability to return to its home site, such as a nest, from distant or unfamiliar places.
A member of the human branch of the primate family tree, including modern people, extinct close relatives and their direct ancestors.
The process by which separate places come to hold increasingly similar sets of organisms, reducing differences between them.
Passing of genes between organisms other than from parent to offspring, a fast route for bacteria to gain new abilities.
A simple model of particles hopping between sites of a lattice and repelling each other when they share a site, used to study strongly interacting electrons.
A mouse given human cells, tissues or genes, often a human immune system, so human disease and treatments can be studied in a living animal.
The part of climate concerned with water: rainfall, evaporation, soil moisture and how dry or wet a region is through the year.
Letting hydrogen atoms in a protein swap with heavier ones from water and weighing the result, which shows which parts are exposed or flexible.
A shortage of oxygen in a tissue. Cells respond by switching on survival and blood-vessel programmes, common in the core of solid tumours.
A cylinder drilled from an ice sheet. Its layers trap old air and chemical traces, giving a dated record of past climate going back thousands of years.
One of two or more versions of a genetic locus that occupy the same position but have unrelated DNA sequences, unlike ordinary alleles, which are similar versions of one gene.
Rock formed when molten rock (magma or lava) cools and solidifies. Slow cooling deep underground gives larger crystals.
A signalling protein released by stressed or infected cells that alerts nearby immune cells and pushes them towards an inflammatory, killing-oriented state.
A drug that blocks brake molecules on immune cells, such as PD-1, letting T cells attack cancer more strongly.
The ways cancer cells or pathogens avoid being recognised or destroyed by the immune system, for example by releasing suppressive signals.
The antibody class secreted onto gut and airway surfaces, where it coats bacteria and shapes which ones thrive.
Inside a living plant, as opposed to in a test tube or in isolated cells.
Performed by computer simulation or analysis rather than in living things or test tubes.
Supplied by a separate molecule rather than being part of the same molecule. For example, a template provided on a different RNA from the enzyme.
A plant or animal strain made genetically almost uniform through many generations of self-crossing or breeding between close relatives.
A sense of direction based on the tilt of the Earth's magnetic field lines relative to the ground rather than on which way is north.
An electron jump between energy levels in a crystal that also needs a lattice vibration to supply momentum. Such jumps absorb and emit light weakly.
A technique that fires neutrons at a sample and measures the energy and momentum they gain or lose, mapping vibrations and magnetic excitations such as magnons.
The tendency of matter to keep its present motion; particles with more of it follow a flow less closely and can be flung out of swirls.
Chronic, low-grade inflammation that develops with age without obvious infection, thought to contribute to many age-related diseases.
A protein complex inside immune cells that senses danger and activates inflammatory signals such as IL-1 beta, sometimes leading to cell death.
A nerve cell that damps down the activity of its partners, usually by releasing GABA or glycine, shaping timing and balance in circuits.
The amount of sunlight reaching a place, which drifts slowly over millennia as Earth's orbit and tilt change, pacing ice ages.
The gradual shrinking of an orbit as energy is lost to drag or gravitational waves, bringing two bodies closer until they merge.
Relating to islands, especially the living things restricted to them and the way isolation shapes their variety.
A quantum jump of electrons from one energy band to another driven by a strong electric field, such as an intense laser pulse.
A gene switched on when cells detect a virus-warning signal; its products block steps of viral replication.
The sensing of the body's own internal state, such as fuel levels, gut activity or heartbeat, and its use by the brain to adjust physiology.
Measuring brain activity from electrodes placed on or in the brain itself, usually during clinical monitoring, giving precise timing and location.
The lasting movement of genetic material from one population or species into another through hybridisation and repeated back-crossing.
A splicing outcome in which an intron stays in the finished messenger RNA, often changing or shortening the protein made.
A plant fibre made of chained fructose units that humans cannot digest but gut bacteria ferment.
Immune-related adverse event: inflammation of normal organs, such as gut, skin, liver or glands, caused by immune checkpoint drugs.
Immune-related colitis: inflammation of the colon caused by immune checkpoint drugs, one of the most common serious side effects of these treatments.
One of several related proteins or transcripts produced from the same gene by different splicing or start sites.
Isoursodeoxycholic acid: a form of the bile acid ursodeoxycholic acid that is produced by gut bacteria.
A unit of a thousand years; written 'ka', it usually means thousands of years before the present when dating fossils and sediments.
Shaping stone, such as flint, by striking off flakes to make tools. Knappable stone breaks in a controlled way suitable for this.
An organism or cell in which a specific gene has been deliberately inactivated, so researchers can see what that gene does.
A material with a regular array of localized magnetic moments that interact with mobile electrons, which can produce heavy electrons and unusual quantum phases.
A gene whose protein relays growth signals inside cells. Mutated versions keep the signal on and drive many pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancers.
The resident macrophage of the liver, lining its blood channels and clearing debris and microbes from blood arriving from the gut.
N-lactoyl-phenylalanine: a molecule formed from lactate and the amino acid phenylalanine. It rises after intense exercise and can reduce food intake.
A form of the enzyme that converts lactate and pyruvate into each other, common in heart muscle where it favours turning lactate into pyruvate.
Copying of the DNA strand that runs the opposite way to the moving replication fork. It is made backwards in short pieces that are later joined.
A thin layer or sheet. Many biological structures stack lamellae at alternating angles for strength, as plywood does.
An immune cell resident in the epidermis that samples substances and microbes in the skin and helps control local immune responses.
A semiconductor compound of lead and sulfur that absorbs infrared light, used in infrared detectors often as tiny crystals.
The lowest-risk category on the IUCN Red List, given to species judged widespread and abundant enough not to be at risk of extinction.
A molecule or ion bound to a central metal atom. Ligands set the metal's shape, colour and reactivity.
A line of descent. In population genetics it names a group sharing ancestry, in cell biology a cell type's developmental path.
Permanently marking a cell so all its descendants carry the mark, revealing where a tissue's cells came from.
A tiny fat-based particle used to carry RNA or other cargo into cells, as in mRNA vaccines.
Damaging oxidation of fats, especially in cell membranes, by reactive molecules. Uncontrolled, it drives ferroptosis.
An electron state confined to a small region rather than spread through the whole material, so it does not carry current.
A specific place in the genome, such as the position of a gene or a DNA region linked to a trait.
Sequencing that reads very long stretches of DNA or RNA in one piece, so whole transcripts and repeats can be resolved.
Describing an experiment designed so that no ordinary explanation remains open, for instance by separating the parts far enough that no signal could pass.
Lipopolysaccharide: a molecule from the outer wall of many bacteria that strongly triggers inflammation. Often used to mimic infection in experiments.
A freshwater fish that breathes air with true lungs and sits close to the ancestry of land vertebrates; some survive dry seasons buried in mud.
Computer methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions, rather than following rules written by hand.
A large ring-shaped molecule. Rings of this size can thread, stack or host other molecules, making them useful building blocks.
A cooperative task in which two separated players must fill entries of a grid consistently; shared quantum resources let them win more often than any classical strategy.
The net strength and direction of a material's internal magnetism per unit volume.
A quantum of a spin wave: a collective ripple in the orientation of electron spins travelling through a magnetic material, carrying energy and spin.
A metal from the outer columns of the periodic table, such as magnesium or calcium, whose bonding uses only s and p electrons.
The thick layer of hot, mostly solid rock between a planet's crust and core. It slowly flows and is the source of most magmas.
A small seabird of the North Atlantic that travels long distances over the ocean and returns reliably to its burrow, making it a model for studying navigation.
A rock that was blasted off Mars by an impact and later fell to Earth. These are the only Martian samples available on Earth.
Training trick in which parts of a sequence are hidden and the model must fill them in, forcing it to learn context and structure.
The yearly difference between snow gained and ice lost by a glacier. A negative balance means it is shrinking.
The minimum energy needed to create an excitation in a system, so no arbitrarily low-energy disturbances exist.
A method that measures the mass of molecules very precisely, used to identify and quantify proteins, peptides and other compounds.
A sensor protein inside cells, related to RIG-I, that recognises long double-stranded viral RNA and starts an interferon-based antiviral response.
The average distance a particle or vibration travels before it is scattered.
A genus of legume plants including alfalfa. Medicago truncatula is a standard model for studying root nodules and nitrogen fixation.
A region with mild wet winters and hot dry summers, found around the Mediterranean and in parts of California, Chile, South Africa and Australia.
The vast, gently sloping fault where one tectonic plate dives under another. These faults host the largest earthquakes.
A microscopy method that labels many different RNA species in intact cells with coded probe rounds, showing which genes are active and where.
A region of actively dividing, undifferentiated plant cells that produces new tissues, such as at root and shoot tips.
A temporary embryonic kidney that forms before the permanent kidney. It largely regresses, but its tissues contribute to the male reproductive ducts and possibly to the gonads.
A pore of intermediate width, wider than a molecule-sized channel but still very small, which lets molecules move quickly through a solid.
Large-scale measurement of the small molecules (metabolites) in a cell, tissue or body fluid, giving a snapshot of chemical activity.
A draft microbial genome pieced together from mixed community sequencing rather than from a single cultured strain.
Sequencing all the DNA in a sample such as gut contents or seawater, so organisms and viruses can be found without growing them in culture.
Light-driven movement of an electron from a metal centre to an attached molecule, the first step in many photochemical reactions.
Any multicellular animal. The term is used to contrast animals with single-celled organisms such as yeast or bacteria.
Addition of a small chemical tag (a methyl group), especially to DNA, which can affect whether nearby genes are switched on.
An early product in the pathway that makes cholesterol and related molecules. Statins block its production.
Cell-surface molecules found on nearly all cells that display short protein fragments from inside the cell to killer T cells.
The whole community of microbes, such as bacteria, viruses and fungi, living in a particular place like the gut, and their genes.
The resident immune cells of the brain and spinal cord. They clear debris, prune connections between nerve cells and react to injury and disease.
The near-weightless condition inside an orbiting craft, where nothing falls relative to its surroundings, so delicate measurements can run far longer than on the ground.
A small multi-cell panel used as an intermediate step between a single laboratory device and a full-size commercial panel.
The small circular genome inside mitochondria. Released into the cell, it acts as a danger signal and sparks inflammation.
The process by which proteins made in the cytoplasm are moved into mitochondria through dedicated membrane channels. Most mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus and need this route.
Opening of the outer mitochondrial membrane during cell death, letting out signals that trigger the cell's self-destruction machinery.
A protein in the inner membrane of mitochondria that imports pyruvate, the product of sugar breakdown, so it can be burned for energy.
A mitochondrion stripped of its outer membrane, used to study what the inner membrane and its proteins do.
The larger-scale interference pattern made when two similar lattices are overlaid with a slight twist or mismatch. In layered crystals it creates a new superlattice that reshapes electron behaviour.
An imaging method that maps the energies and directions of electrons knocked out of a material by light, revealing how electrons move inside it.
A membrane transport protein that carries lactate, pyruvate and similar small molecules into or out of cells.
A material that should conduct according to simple band theory but insulates because strong repulsion between electrons stops them from moving onto already occupied sites.
A cell line taken from an early mouse embryo that can grow indefinitely and give rise to nearly every body tissue, used to build genetically altered animals.
The main receptor through which morphine and similar drugs relieve pain. It also mediates their side effects, such as breathing depression and dependence.
Combining several large-scale molecular measurements, such as genes, RNA, proteins and metabolites, from the same samples to get a fuller picture.
A combined measure of variety across many unrelated groups of organisms at once, rather than counting kinds within a single group.
A relationship between two species in which both benefit.

A family of two-dimensional materials made of thin layers of transition metal carbides or nitrides, usually made by etching out a layer from a parent crystal. Studied for batteries, electronics and shielding.
A master gene whose protein drives cell growth and division. It is overactive in many cancers and has long resisted direct drugging.
The blood-cell family that includes monocytes, macrophages and neutrophils. In tumours these cells often suppress rather than help immune attack.
A very small antibody fragment, originally from camels, that binds a target and reaches pockets full-sized antibodies cannot.
A channel or pore only a few nanometres wide, through which ions or molecules pass. Such channels are used in filtration and separation membranes.
A diamond particle only nanometres across, extremely stiff and chemically inert, used as a filler or as a carrier of optical defects.
A strip of material only a few nanometres wide, such as a narrow strip of graphene, whose electronic properties depend on its width and edges.
A lymphocyte that kills stressed, infected or tumour cells without needing to be primed against a specific target first.
A chemical made by a living organism, often with complex structure and biological activity; many antibiotics and cancer drugs come from this source.
A serious bowel disease mainly of premature newborns in which parts of the gut wall become inflamed and die.
A pattern of colour or markings on a flower, often visible only in ultraviolet light, that leads visiting insects or birds towards the nectar.
A plant gland, usually in the flower, that produces and releases nectar to attract and reward pollinating animals.
A family of surface proteins that help neighbouring cells stick together. Several viruses hijack them as doorways into the cell.
A new protein fragment, not normally made by the body, that the immune system can see as foreign. Often arises from mutations in cancer.
The geological era roughly one billion to half a billion years ago, ending just before animals diversified, marked by severe global glaciations.
A pattern in which poorer sites hold a subset of the organisms found at richer ones, so differences come from losses rather than replacements.
A filament protein made by dividing neural stem and progenitor cells, widely used as a marker to target or identify them.
A dividing cell of the developing brain that gives rise to neurons and glia, widely used to study early brain development in a dish.
A nickel-titanium alloy with shape memory and springiness, already used in stents, orthodontic wires and bone staples.
Conversion of nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia, a form living things can use. Some bacteria do this, often in partnership with plants.
A sensor protein that forms the best-known inflammasome, responding to many danger signals and linked to gout, atherosclerosis and age-related inflammation.
A small growth on the roots of legumes where nitrogen-fixing bacteria live and work in partnership with the plant.
A type of jumping genetic element, such as LINE-1, that lacks long repeated ends and inserts its copy by reverse transcribing its RNA directly at the target DNA site.
A transcription factor that switches on many antioxidant and detoxifying genes when cells face oxidative stress.
A young stage of an insect that already resembles the adult but lacks full wings and cannot yet breed.
An insect of the order Odonata, the dragonflies and damselflies. Their larvae live in water, making them useful indicators of freshwater health.
A short piece of DNA made on the lagging strand during replication. Many such pieces are later joined into one continuous strand.
Building molecules directly on a clean metal surface, often under vacuum, to make structures too large or reactive to make in solution.
A trap that holds neutral atoms in the focus of a laser beam, working for atoms that magnetic traps cannot hold.
A method that makes chosen nerve cells sensitive to light by giving them light-gated proteins, so researchers can switch them on or off with light.
The region around an atom or molecule where an electron is likely to be found, with a set energy. How these regions overlap and mix decides how atoms bond.
Rotation carried by the twisting shape of a light beam's wavefront, separate from the spinning associated with its polarisation.
Nitrogen held in carbon-containing compounds such as amino acids or urea, rather than in simple mineral forms.
Speeding up reactions with compounds in which calcium is bonded to carbon-based groups, offering a cheap, abundant alternative to precious metals.
An organic compound containing a carbon-chlorine bond. Many are cheap and stable but hard to activate for chemical reactions.
A small three-dimensional tissue grown from stem cells or a patient sample that reproduces some structure of a real organ or tumour.
The same gene in two different species, inherited from their common ancestor and usually doing a similar job.
The main way mitochondria make the cell's energy currency, ATP, using oxygen and a chain of membrane proteins.
A form of oxygen atom with a different number of neutrons, such as oxygen-16 or oxygen-18. Their ratios act as fingerprints of a sample's origin, temperature or water history.
A recently proposed kind of magnet with no overall magnetisation, in which electrons moving in opposite directions carry opposite spin, giving spin-dependent effects without stray fields.
A voltage-gated calcium channel at many nerve endings. Calcium entry through it triggers release of chemical messengers.
A stress-activated signalling enzyme inside cells that passes on alarm signals such as damage, inflammation or salt imbalance and changes which genes are switched on.
A lake that existed in the past but has since dried up, often leaving sediments that record former wetter climates.
Identifying ancient proteins surviving in fossils such as teeth or bone, which can reveal species and sex when DNA has decayed away.
The upper part of the vertebrate forebrain. In mammals it forms the cerebral cortex; in birds it is organised differently but supports comparable complex cognition.
Attachment of a fatty acid to a protein, a reversible tag that tethers the protein to membranes and switches its activity.
Describing an analysis that pools many different cancer types to find features they share rather than studying one organ at a time.
The combined set of genes found across many individuals or species of a group, capturing variation that a single reference sequence misses.
A symmetry in which a system behaves the same when added electrons are swapped for missing electrons (holes). When broken, electron- and hole-rich states behave differently.
Treating a surface so that defects there stop trapping charge carriers or reacting, which raises device efficiency and lifetime.
No remaining invasive cancer found in tissue removed at surgery after treatment given beforehand.
A model in which tumour tissue from a patient is grown in an immunodeficient mouse, keeping much of the original tumour's features.
A brake receptor on T cells that weakens their activity when bound by its partner molecules. Drugs blocking it are used in cancer immunotherapy.
A surface protein that switches off attacking T cells. Tumours use it to hide, and antibodies against it release the brake.
A long-predicted form of carbon sheet made of five- and seven-membered rings instead of graphene's six-membered rings.
A choice based on interpreting sensory information, such as judging whether a stimulus is present or which category it belongs to.
A protein released by killer T cells and natural killer cells that punches pores in the membrane of target cells.
Around the portal tracts of the liver, where incoming blood vessels and bile ducts run.
A sensor in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane that detects unfolded proteins and slows protein synthesis in response.
A family of crystals sharing one atomic arrangement. Lead-halide versions absorb light strongly and make cheap, efficient solar cells.
The study of rocks: their minerals, textures, origin and history.
The geological eon from about half a billion years ago to today, covering the whole record of abundant animal fossils.
A sudden local unwinding of the shared quantum phase in a superconductor or superfluid, which costs energy and shows up as resistance.
A simulation approach that describes regions of different structure using smoothly varying fields, letting patterns and boundaries evolve in a model.
A chemical released by an animal that changes the behaviour of others of its kind, for example in attracting mates.
Phenome-wide association study: testing a genetic variant against many traits and diseases at once to find all the outcomes it is linked to.
The smallest unit of sound that distinguishes one word from another in a language.
A quantum of lattice vibration, the main carrier of heat in insulating crystals.
A highly toxic gas used in industry to make plastics and chemicals. Safer liquid or solid chemicals are often used in its place.
A chemical link joining phosphate to a carbon-containing group, found in DNA backbones, many signalling molecules and detergents.
The science and technology of generating, guiding and detecting light, as in lasers, optical fibres and light-based chips.
Measurement of blood volume changes in the skin using light, the technique behind the pulse and heart-rate readings of watches and finger clips.
A drug-like molecule that changes shape when light of a certain colour hits it, so its activity can be switched on or off with light.
A plant light-sensing protein that measures red and far-red light and uses it to time germination, growth and flowering.
A fin-footed marine mammal such as a seal, sea lion or walrus.
An enzyme activated by double-stranded RNA during viral infection. It shuts down protein production in the cell, which helps block virus replication.
One small repeating cell of a lattice pattern, used as the unit for counting trapped charges or fluxes in a periodic structure.
A clinical trial that tests several treatments under one shared plan, allowing arms to be added or dropped over time.
A swirl in which the electric dipoles of a material curl around a centre, forming a stable pattern in thin oxide layers.
Having more than two full sets of chromosomes, a common condition in plants that can arise from hybridisation or failed cell division.
A fatty acid with several double bonds. These are flexible in membranes but prone to oxidative damage.
A widely used, chlorine-containing plastic found in pipes, cables and medical tubing.
The vast grassland belt north of the Black and Caspian Seas, home to herding peoples whose ancestry later spread widely across Eurasia.
A ring-shaped protein assembly set in a viral shell that forms a channel through which genetic material or other molecules can pass.
The retention by adult cells of gene activity that reflects where in the body they came from, helping guide regeneration to restore the right structures.
A baby's age counted from the first day of the mother's last menstrual period, so it equals gestational age plus time since birth. Used to track preterm infants.
A family of large brick-shaped DNA viruses that replicate in the cell fluid rather than the nucleus; smallpox and vaccinia belong to it.
A nuclear receptor that senses fat molecules and controls fat-cell formation and insulin sensitivity; the target of glitazone drugs.
The first RNA copy of a gene, still containing non-coding stretches that must be cut out before it can be used to make protein.
Stretch already present in a material before any outside load is applied, which changes how it shares the load later.
A food ingredient that is not digested by the host but feeds helpful gut bacteria, in contrast to swallowing the bacteria themselves.
A small second phase that forms inside a solid alloy. Precipitates strengthen the metal and can hold or release dissolved atoms.
A violent early stage after rapid expansion in the early Universe in which energy stored in a field is dumped into particles.
Attachment of a small branched hydrocarbon to a molecule, which can anchor proteins to membranes or build plant natural products.
Publicly recording a study's hypotheses and analysis plan before seeing the data, to reduce selective reporting and false findings.
A stage in which a disturbed quantum system settles into a long-lived, almost steady state before it finally reaches true thermal equilibrium.
A mitochondrial scaffold protein that organises the inner membrane and helps control shape, quality and cell death.
A lipid signalling molecule made from arachidonic acid by cyclooxygenase enzymes. It regulates inflammation, fever, pain and the growth of many cell types.
A visible clump of misfolded or aggregated protein inside a cell, often seen in brain cells in neurodegenerative diseases.
Physical contact between two proteins, the basis of most cell signalling. Drugs may block such contacts or force them to form.
The full set of proteins an organism can make. It outnumbers the genes, because one gene can be read out as several different protein forms.
Large-scale study of the proteins in a cell or tissue, usually measured by mass spectrometry, including their amounts and modifications.
The balance of making, folding, maintaining and breaking down proteins in a cell, which keeps the protein supply healthy.
A mostly single-celled organism with a nucleus that is not an animal, plant or fungus, such as an amoeba or a ciliate.
Tagging whatever sits close to a chosen protein inside living cells, so its neighbours can be pulled out and identified.
Discrete, sharply separated electron energy levels that appear when strain in a crystal mimics the effect of a strong magnetic field.
A partial dip in the available electron states, seen in copper-oxide superconductors above the temperature at which they superconduct.
A large neuron with a highly branched, fan-shaped dendrite tree in the cerebellar cortex. It provides the only output of the cerebellar cortex and is key for motor coordination.
An immune sensor protein that forms an inflammasome when certain cell signalling pathways are disturbed. Mutations in its gene cause familial Mediterranean fever.
An inflammatory form of programmed cell death, triggered by inflammasomes, in which the cell bursts and releases inflammatory signals.
A jump between atomic energy levels driven by how the field varies across the atom rather than by its average value, so it is weak and narrow.
Electrical conduction confined to a material's edges, with no magnetic field needed, arising from the material's own magnetism and band structure.
The theory of the strong force that binds quarks into protons and neutrons, using three colour charges.
The ability of a quantum system to keep a well-defined combination of states over time. Losing it destroys stored quantum information.
A link between separated systems such that measuring one immediately constrains what can be found for the other, with no classical counterpart.
Imaging ultracold atoms in a lattice one site at a time, so each particle's position and type can be read off directly.
A network that links quantum devices with light so they can share quantum information, for secure communication or distributed quantum computing.
Suddenly changing a control parameter of a quantum system and watching how it evolves far from equilibrium.
A well-controlled set of atoms, ions or circuits arranged to act out a model of another quantum system that is too hard to compute.
A carbon atom bonded to four other carbon atoms; building one with a defined three-dimensional arrangement is a classic synthetic challenge.
The basic unit of quantum information. Unlike a normal bit, it can be in a mix of 0 and 1 at the same time.
A molecule or atom with an unpaired electron, making it highly reactive. Radical reactions are used to build bonds and make plastics.
Two molecules each carrying an unpaired electron, created together so their spins stay linked; reactions between them can be sensitive to magnetic fields.
An age estimate for rock or sediment obtained from the steady decay of radioactive atoms it contains.
Any of the 17 metallic elements made up of scandium, yttrium and the lanthanides. They have unusual magnetic and optical properties and are used in magnets and electronics.
A DNA difference carried by only a small share of people, usually under about one percent. Single ones can have larger effects but are hard to study statistically.
An electronic chip under an image sensor that collects and processes the signal from each pixel.
A change in RNA, such as by editing, that alters which amino acid is coded, so the resulting protein differs from the DNA's instructions.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature's global inventory of threatened species, the main list that ranks species by extinction risk, from Least Concern to Extinct.
A stretch of DNA that does not code for protein but controls when, where and how strongly nearby genes are switched on.
A hormone of the insulin family that relaxes connective tissue and blood vessels and limits scarring, best known from pregnancy.
The large group of proteins that work together at the replication fork to unwind DNA and copy both strands.
Starch that escapes digestion in the small intestine and reaches the colon, where bacteria ferment it.
A spectroscopy that tunes X-rays to an energy that a chosen atom absorbs strongly and measures the energy they lose on scattering, revealing electronic and magnetic excitations such as magnons.
Building solids by linking molecular units into regular, net-like frameworks, usually with predictable pores and geometry.
An output neuron of the retina whose fibre carries visual signals to the brain; distinct kinds report different features.
A DNA segment that copies itself through an RNA step and inserts the new copy elsewhere in the genome. Such elements make up much of many genomes.
Soil bacteria that live in root nodules of legumes such as beans and turn nitrogen gas into forms the plant can use.
A slip of the protein-making machinery onto a shifted reading frame, so the same stretch of RNA yields a different protein.
A zone where the Earth's crust is being pulled apart, forming a long valley that may eventually split a continent and open a new ocean.
A sensor protein inside cells that detects viral RNA and triggers an antiviral response, including production of type I interferons.
Changing specific letters in an RNA after it is made from DNA, so the protein produced can differ from what the gene encodes.
A barrel-shaped machine that chews up unwanted or faulty RNA, controlling how much of each transcript survives.
The way an RNA strand pairs with itself to form loops and stems; the resulting shape affects its stability, location and handling by proteins.
Reactive oxygen species: highly reactive oxygen-containing molecules made during normal metabolism and stress. They signal at low levels and cause damage at high levels.
A cell-surface receptor with a large external portion that senses a hormone of the insulin family and triggers signalling inside the cell.
The region of a plant genome that controls self-incompatibility. It carries matching pollen and pistil genes whose many variants decide which pollen is rejected.
A bacterium that invades the lining of the intestine, causing food-borne diarrhoeal illness in people and a typhoid-like disease in mice.
The major fault in California where the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other horizontally, causing frequent earthquakes.
Imaging methods that move a very sharp tip over a surface to map it, down to single atoms and their electronic states.
A technique that scans a sharp metal tip just above a conducting surface and measures the tiny quantum tunnelling current, imaging individual atoms and electronic states.
A line defect in a crystal where the layers are displaced in a spiral around it, so following a loop steps you up one layer.
A condition stating which jumps between quantum states are allowed, set by conservation of angular momentum and symmetry.
A single, spontaneously ordered layer of molecules anchored to a surface, used to tune how charge crosses that interface.
A genetic system in many flowering plants that stops pollen from fertilising the same plant or close relatives, promoting outbreeding.
A pair of European satellites that photograph the land surface in several colour bands every few days at fine resolution, widely used to track vegetation.
Holding a molecule inside a compartment or assembly so it is kept away from the machinery that would normally use or destroy it.
A metal that can be deformed and then snap back to its original shape, releasing or absorbing heat as its crystal structure switches.
A measure of how strongly a material resists sliding deformation, where one face is pushed sideways relative to another; low values mean a very soft solid.
Random fluctuation in a current because charge arrives in discrete lumps. Its size reveals how large those lumps are.
A flexible, heat-stable polymer with a backbone of alternating silicon and oxygen atoms, used in oils, rubbers, sealants and medical implants.
A highly reactive, positively charged silicon species that strongly grabs electron-rich atoms such as oxygen and chlorine.
A standard mathematical model of a field with a periodic energy landscape, used to study waves, kinks and tunnelling in many physical settings.
The short RNA that tells a CRISPR protein which DNA sequence to bind, so one protein can be aimed at any chosen site.
Methods that measure two or more kinds of molecular data, such as RNA and open chromatin, from the same individual cell, linking gene control to gene activity.
A method that reads which genes are active in thousands of individual cells, so cell types and states can be told apart.
Microscopy methods that track individual molecules one at a time, often with fluorescent labels, to see how they move and interact.
A device in which one molecule bridges two electrodes, so electric current through that single molecule can be measured.
A common difference at a single DNA letter between people. Such markers are used to map genes linked to traits and diseases.
Reading the gene activity of individual cell nuclei isolated from tissue, which allows frozen or fragile samples such as brain to be profiled one cell at a time.
Measuring how X-rays deflect slightly off a sample to reveal structures of nanometre size, such as the spacing inside collagen fibrils.
The share of differences in a trait between people that can be explained by common DNA markers measured together across the genome.
A flaw in a crystal, such as a missing atom next to a foreign atom, that can trap electrons and act as a qubit.
A set of methods that measure which genes are active in tissue while keeping track of where each cell or spot sits in the section.
How steeply the number of kinds of organism rises as the area surveyed grows; steeper values mean larger places hold disproportionately more variety.
A standard measure of a light detector's sensitivity that adjusts for its size and bandwidth, measured in units called Jones. Higher means fainter signals can be seen.
A cave mineral deposit such as a stalagmite. Its layers can be dated precisely and record past rainfall and temperature.
A flow of electron spin, the tiny magnetic property of electrons, which may occur with or without a flow of electric charge.
A large group of atoms or defects whose magnetic moments act together as one collective system, often coupled to a resonator.
An imbalance between the two possible magnetic orientations of electrons, so a current or a state carries net magnetic character.
A device of magnetic layers whose electrical resistance depends on how their magnetizations line up, used to detect and inject spin currents.
Knocking electrons out of a crystal with light and measuring both their energy and direction and their magnetic orientation, mapping electronic states.
A system that links a quantum spin, which stores information, with particles of light, which carry it, so quantum information can be transferred.
Electronics that use electron spin, not just charge, to store and process information, as in computer hard-disk read heads and magnetic memory.
A transcription factor that senses cholesterol levels and switches on genes for making and taking up cholesterol when levels are low.
Measuring ratios of heavy to light atoms in a sample to infer diet, water source or climate at the time it formed.
Genetic ancestry traced to herders of the Eurasian grasslands who spread widely into Europe and Asia in the Bronze Age.
A spatial transcriptomics method that captures RNA on a chip of DNA-barcoded spots, mapping gene activity across a tissue section at very fine resolution.
An atom, usually carbon, carrying groups arranged so that swapping any two of them gives a different molecule that cannot be laid exactly over the original.
A family of cells, sharing a developmental origin, that become able to make steroid hormones such as testosterone, oestrogen or cortisol, as in the gonads and adrenal glands.
A deep brain region in the basal ganglia involved in movement control, habits and reward. It is the area most damaged in Huntington's disease.
A large change in DNA structure, usually at least 50 base pairs, such as a deletion, duplication, insertion or inversion.
Combining many copies of the same structure cut out of three-dimensional electron images to raise detail and reveal fine features.
A group of cells within one tumour that share extra mutations, so a single tumour contains several genetically distinct populations.
The process at converging plate boundaries in which one tectonic plate sinks beneath another into the mantle, creating deep trenches, volcanoes and large earthquakes.
A small version of a full solar panel, made of several connected cells, used to test how a laboratory result scales up.
An animal's use of the Sun's position, corrected for time of day by its internal clock, to hold a travel direction.
Flow without friction in a cold quantum fluid. Colour superfluidity is a proposed version involving three kinds of particle.
A layered midbrain structure that maps visual space and drives orienting movements of eyes and head.
A ridge along the upper side of the temporal lobe, central to hearing and to recognising speech sounds.
A larger-scale repeating pattern built on top of a crystal's own lattice, which reshapes how electrons move and what energies they can take.
Light or microwave emission that becomes much brighter and faster because many atoms radiate together in step instead of independently.
A type of mobile repeated DNA sequence found only in humans and other great apes that can insert itself into genes and disturb how they are read.
An organism living in close, long-term association with another organism of a different species, often inside its cells or tissues.
How strongly activity in one neuron drives its partner across a connection; raising it makes a circuit respond more to the same input.
The fused outer cell layer of the placenta that faces maternal blood and controls what passes between mother and fetus.
A membrane protein of the SNARE family that helps vesicles fuse with the cell membrane, which is needed for release of nerve messengers.
A partnership in which two microbes depend on each other to feed, often because one uses the waste products of the other.
The surface receptor that lets a T cell recognize a specific protein fragment displayed by MHC molecules.
A short DNA sequence repeated many times in a row. The number of repeats often differs between people and can change how nearby genes work.
Two light-absorbing layers stacked so each takes a different part of the spectrum, raising efficiency beyond a single layer.
A short DNA sequence just upstream of many genes that helps position the machinery starting the copying of the gene into RNA.
A small sulfur-containing molecule found in high amounts in many tissues and in the diet. It has roles in bile, cell volume and protection against stress.
