Sending measurements from a sensor to a distant reader without a wired link, for example by light or radio.
The front-most part of the vertebrate brain, which forms the cerebral hemispheres in mammals and their counterparts in birds and fish.
A unit of mass equal to a million tonnes, commonly used for global budgets of elements such as nitrogen or carbon.
Holding a flying insect in place while it beats its wings, so the direction it tries to head can be recorded under controlled conditions.
A type of helper T cell that makes the signal protein IL-17. It helps fight some bacteria and fungi but also drives many inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, such as psoriasis.
How readily a material conducts heat. The transverse component describes heat flowing sideways to the applied gradient.
A sideways flow of heat that appears at right angles to an applied temperature difference in a magnetic field.
Breeding a population at a chosen temperature over generations so that variants coping better with it become more common.
Internal forces that build up when joined materials expand or shrink by different amounts as temperature changes, which can crack or peel interfaces.
A driven system that settles into a pattern repeating in time at a rhythm different from the one pushing it, much as an ordinary crystal repeats in space.
A gene whose protein partners with another clock protein to keep the daily internal rhythm of insects running.
A memory T cell that stays in one tissue, such as skin or gut, instead of circulating in blood. It reacts fast to a repeat threat but can also keep local inflammation going.
A local flaw in an ordered pattern that cannot be smoothed away. Enough of them can melt the order entirely.
The exit side of the Golgi apparatus, where newly made proteins and fats are sorted into packages and sent to their destinations.
A label, often a modified virus, that spreads from one neuron across its connection to the next, revealing which cells are wired together.
The full set of RNA molecules present in a cell or tissue at one time, read out to show which genes are active.
A small RNA molecule that carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome and matches it to the code in messenger RNA during protein synthesis.
A cell-surface protein that binds transferrin, the blood protein that carries iron, and brings it into the cell.
The part of a protein that sits within the cell membrane, anchoring it and often passing signals from outside to inside.
The release of chemical messengers from a nerve ending when vesicles fuse with its membrane, passing a signal to the next cell.
A single charged atom held in place by electric fields in vacuum, used as a precisely controlled quantum system.
Regulatory T cell: a T cell that dampens immune responses and prevents attacks on the body's own tissues. Usually marked by the protein FOXP3.
The cell type that forms the placenta, attaching the pregnancy to the womb and handling exchange with maternal blood.
The mixture of non-cancer cells, blood vessels, immune cells and surrounding material in which a tumour grows and which shapes its behaviour.
Irregular, swirling fluid motion across many scales, which mixes momentum and suspended material far faster than smooth flow.
The replacement of one set of things by a different set between places or over time, such as species between sites or DNA elements over evolution, rather than simple gain or loss.
The small rotation between two stacked atomic layers. It sets the pattern they form together and strongly changes the electronic behaviour.
A small protein attached to other proteins as a tag that can mark them for breakdown or change their activity or location.
Attachment of ubiquitin tags to a protein, which can mark it for breakdown or change its function. Also called ubiquitination.
A large British research resource of about half a million volunteers with genetic data, health records, scans and samples, open to researchers.
A stretch of DNA kept almost unchanged across distant species, a strong hint that it does something important.
The parts of a messenger RNA flanking the protein-coding stretch. They control where the RNA goes and how much protein is made.
A large DNA virus of the smallpox family, used as the smallpox vaccine and as a laboratory model and vector.
A sandwich built by laying atomically thin crystal sheets on one another, held together only by weak surface attraction rather than chemical bonds.
A signal that tells blood-vessel lining cells to grow and sprout. Drugs blocking it are used in cancer and eye disease.
A surface-science method that fires short pulses of molecules at a surface and times when they leave, measuring their speed, to work out reaction rates and binding energies.
A small midbrain region packed with dopamine-making neurons that signal reward and drive learning about what is worth repeating.
A complete virus particle outside a cell: the genetic material wrapped in its protein shell and, in some families, a membrane.
Behaviour that is part springy and part flowing, so a material springs back at once and then keeps slowly deforming under the same load.
The ability to learn new sounds by hearing and copying others, as in human speech and songbird song. Most animals have only inborn calls.
A compound that evaporates easily at ordinary temperatures, so it travels through air and can be smelled or sensed at a distance.
A pore in the outer mitochondrial membrane that lets small molecules in and out and opens or closes with voltage.
An exercise model in which rodents can run on a wheel in their cage as much as they choose, rather than being forced.
A swirl of circulating flow or of a material's internal orientation around a central line, often carrying a fixed quantised amount of rotation.
A light beam with a helical wavefront and a dark centre, which carries twist and can set small objects turning.
Reliable access to enough safe water for people, farming, industry and nature, which depends on infrastructure, management and demand, not only on rainfall.
Reading the complete DNA sequence of an organism's genome, including the non-coding regions between genes.
A solid-like arrangement in which electrons, kept apart by their mutual repulsion, settle into a regular lattice. It forms when repulsion outweighs their kinetic energy at low density.
A cell communication system that controls growth, development and stem cell maintenance. Abnormal activity is common in cancer.
Carried on the X chromosome. Because the sexes carry different numbers of X chromosomes, such genes can act unequally in males and females.
An inherited adult-onset movement disorder affecting mainly men, in which twisting postures and later stiffness and slowness develop as brain cells are lost.
A machine that whips free electrons through magnets to make extremely bright, extremely short X-ray flashes for imaging fast events.
A genus of African clawed frogs. Their large eggs and egg extracts are widely used to study development, cell division and DNA replication.
A transcription co-activator controlled by the Hippo pathway and by cell crowding and stiffness. It helps cells sense their surroundings and decide whether to grow.
A crystalline framework of silicon, aluminium and oxygen riddled with regular molecule-sized channels, used as a catalyst and molecular sieve.
Producing a working result on the first attempt, without examples of the specific task or rounds of trial-and-error improvement.
A unit of length equal to one ten-billionth of a metre, about the size of an atom. Used for atomic distances and crystal spacings.
